topic: a lighthouse keeper's last night
title: A última noite do farol
text:
Durante quarenta anos, seu Joaquim cuidou do farol de uma pequena ilha no litoral de Santa Catarina. Todas as tardes, subia os degraus da torre, limpava o vidro e acendia a luz que guiava os barcos dos pescadores. Mas, a partir do dia seguinte, o farol ia funcionar sozinho, controlado por um computador no continente.

Na última noite, Joaquim fez tudo como sempre, mas bem devagar. Olhando o mar escuro, pensou: “Amanhã ninguém vai se lembrar de mim. Uma máquina vai fazer o meu trabalho.” Ele se sentia velho e inútil.

Perto da meia-noite, porém, viu uma luz no mar. Depois, outra e mais outra. Logo, dezenas de barcos cercavam a ilha, todos com as lanternas acesas. Eram os pescadores da vila. Pelo rádio, uma voz conhecida disse: “Seu Joaquim, por quarenta anos o senhor iluminou o nosso caminho. Hoje é a nossa vez.” O velho não conseguiu responder. Apenas acendeu e apagou a luz do farol três vezes, como um abraço.
translation:
For forty years, Seu Joaquim looked after the lighthouse on a small island off the coast of Santa Catarina. Every afternoon, he climbed the steps of the tower, cleaned the glass and switched on the light that guided the fishermen's boats. But from the next day on, the lighthouse was going to work on its own, controlled by a computer on the mainland.

On the last night, Joaquim did everything as always, but very slowly. Looking at the dark sea, he thought: “Tomorrow nobody will remember me. A machine is going to do my job.” He felt old and useless.

Around midnight, however, he saw a light on the sea. Then another, and another. Soon dozens of boats surrounded the island, all with their lanterns lit. They were the fishermen from the village. Over the radio, a familiar voice said: “Seu Joaquim, for forty years you lit our way. Today it's our turn.” The old man couldn't answer. He just switched the lighthouse light on and off three times, like a hug.

questions.q: What is the story mainly about?
options: A fisherman who gets lost at sea at night
A lighthouse keeper's last night at work
A village that builds a new lighthouse
A boy who visits an island with his family
questions.explain: The story follows Joaquim, who looked after the lighthouse for forty years, on 'a última noite'.

questions.q: Why was it Joaquim's last night at the lighthouse?
options: He was moving to the mainland to live with family
The fishermen had asked for a younger keeper
The old tower was going to be closed for repairs
The light would be controlled by a computer
questions.explain: The text says the lighthouse 'ia funcionar sozinho, controlado por um computador no continente'.

questions.q: How did Joaquim feel before midnight?
options: Old and useless
Proud and excited
Free and relaxed
Angry and afraid
questions.explain: The text says 'Ele se sentia velho e inútil'.

questions.q: What did the voice on the radio mean by “Hoje é a nossa vez”?
options: It was their turn to move to the island
It was their turn to look after the tower
It was their turn to light the way for him
It was their turn to go out fishing at night
questions.explain: The voice says Joaquim lit their way for forty years ('o senhor iluminou o nosso caminho'), so now they light his.

topic: how coffee arrived in Brazil
title: Um buquê muito especial
text:
O café não é uma planta nativa do Brasil. As primeiras mudas chegaram a Belém, no Pará, em 1727, trazidas por Francisco de Melo Palheta, que voltava da Guiana Francesa. Conta-se que os franceses proibiam a saída de café da colônia, mas a esposa do governador deu a Palheta um buquê de flores. Escondidas entre as flores, havia sementes e pequenas mudas.

No Norte, porém, a produção continuou pequena. O café só prosperou quando chegou ao Rio de Janeiro e, depois, a São Paulo e Minas Gerais, onde encontrou temperaturas amenas e chuvas regulares. No século XIX, as fazendas se multiplicaram, e o Brasil se tornou o maior produtor do mundo, posição que mantém até hoje.

O dinheiro do café transformou o país. Foram construídas ferrovias para levar os sacos até o porto de Santos, e São Paulo, que era uma cidade pequena, virou um grande centro. Hoje, oferecer um cafezinho às visitas é um gesto de boas-vindas em quase toda casa brasileira.
translation:
Coffee is not a plant native to Brazil. The first seedlings arrived in Belém, in Pará, in 1727, brought by Francisco de Melo Palheta, who was returning from French Guiana. It is said that the French prohibited coffee from leaving the colony, but the governor's wife gave Palheta a bouquet of flowers. Hidden among the flowers were seeds and small seedlings.

In the North, however, production remained small. Coffee only prospered when it reached Rio de Janeiro and, later, São Paulo and Minas Gerais, where it found mild temperatures and regular rain. In the 19th century, farms multiplied, and Brazil became the world's largest producer, a position it still holds today.

Coffee money transformed the country. Railways were built to carry the sacks to the port of Santos, and São Paulo, which was a small city, became a major centre. Today, offering a cafezinho to visitors is a gesture of welcome in almost every Brazilian home.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why coffee grows best in the north of Brazil
How Brazilians prepare a good cafezinho
How coffee came to Brazil and changed it
Why the French stopped growing coffee
questions.explain: The passage tells how the first coffee plants reached Brazil in 1727 and says 'O dinheiro do café transformou o país'.

questions.q: According to the story, how did Palheta get the coffee plants?
options: They were hidden in a bouquet of flowers
He bought them at a market in Belém
He found them growing near a river
The governor sent them to Brazil by ship
questions.explain: The governor's wife gave him flowers, and 'Escondidas entre as flores, havia sementes e pequenas mudas'.

questions.q: Where did coffee first grow really well in Brazil?
options: In Rio, then São Paulo and Minas Gerais
In Pará and the other states of the North
Only around the port city of Belém
In the forests near French Guiana
questions.explain: The text says 'O café só prosperou quando chegou ao Rio de Janeiro e, depois, a São Paulo e Minas Gerais'.

questions.q: What does “posição que mantém até hoje” tell us?
options: Brazil produced coffee only in the 19th century
Brazil lost its first place after the railways
Coffee farms today are in the same places as before
Brazil is still the world's largest coffee producer
questions.explain: The phrase follows 'o maior produtor do mundo', so Brazil keeps that first place today.

topic: Portuguese pavement and Copacabana's waves
title: Ondas de pedra
text:
Quem caminha pela orla de Copacabana, no Rio de Janeiro, pisa em uma obra de arte. O famoso calçadão, com ondas pretas e brancas, é feito de calçada portuguesa: milhões de pedrinhas de basalto, que é preto, e de calcário, que é branco, colocadas uma a uma, à mão, por trabalhadores chamados calceteiros.

A técnica nasceu em Portugal. Em meados do século XIX, a Praça do Rossio, em Lisboa, ganhou um desenho de ondas que imitava o mar. A ideia atravessou o oceano com calceteiros portugueses e, no começo do século XX, um desenho parecido foi escolhido para Copacabana.

Além de bonita, a calçada portuguesa é prática: a água da chuva passa pelos espaços entre as pedras e penetra no solo, e um buraco pode ser consertado sem quebrar o resto do chão. O problema é que o trabalho é lento e cansativo, e hoje há cada vez menos calceteiros. Em muitas cidades, essa arte corre o risco de desaparecer.
translation:
Anyone who walks along the Copacabana seafront, in Rio de Janeiro, steps on a work of art. The famous promenade, with its black and white waves, is made of Portuguese pavement: millions of little stones of basalt, which is black, and limestone, which is white, placed one by one, by hand, by workers called calceteiros.

The technique was born in Portugal. In the mid-19th century, Rossio Square, in Lisbon, got a wave design that imitated the sea. The idea crossed the ocean with Portuguese calceteiros and, at the beginning of the 20th century, a similar design was chosen for Copacabana.

Besides being beautiful, Portuguese pavement is practical: rainwater passes through the spaces between the stones and soaks into the ground, and a hole can be repaired without breaking the rest of the pavement. The problem is that the work is slow and tiring, and today there are fewer and fewer calceteiros. In many cities, this art is at risk of disappearing.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The history of Copacabana and its hotels
How modern cities build their sidewalks
Why Brazilians prefer black and white art
A traditional stone pavement and its story
questions.explain: The whole passage is about the black and white stone pavement of the Copacabana promenade.

questions.q: How are the stones put in place?
options: A machine presses them into the ground
They are glued onto large boards first
Workers place them one by one, by hand
They come in big ready-made squares
questions.explain: The stones are 'colocadas uma a uma, à mão, por trabalhadores chamados calceteiros'.

questions.q: Why is the pavement practical, according to the passage?
options: It never becomes slippery in the rain
Rainwater can go down into the ground
Its stones are cheaper than concrete
It can be laid much faster than asphalt
questions.explain: The text says 'a água da chuva passa pelos espaços entre as pedras e penetra no solo'.

questions.q: What can we conclude about the wave design in Copacabana?
options: It was created by Brazilian painters
It was inspired by a design from Lisbon
It was copied later by squares in Lisbon
It shows a map of the city of Rio
questions.explain: Rossio Square in Lisbon got a wave design in the 19th century, and later 'um desenho parecido foi escolhido para Copacabana'.

topic: leaf-cutter ants farming fungus
title: As formigas agricultoras
text:
Quem anda por uma trilha no Brasil provavelmente já viu uma fila de formigas carregando pedaços de folhas. São as saúvas, ou formigas-cortadeiras. Cada uma leva um pedaço de folha muito maior do que o próprio corpo. Muita gente acha que elas comem essas folhas, mas não é verdade.

As folhas vão para o formigueiro, que pode ter centenas de câmaras subterrâneas. Lá, as formigas mastigam as folhas e fazem uma espécie de massa. Sobre essa massa cresce um fungo, e é esse fungo que alimenta a colônia. Ou seja, as saúvas são agricultoras: cultivam a própria comida, e fazem isso há milhões de anos, muito antes dos seres humanos.

Cada formiga tem uma tarefa. As maiores defendem o ninho, as médias cortam e carregam as folhas, e as menores cuidam da plantação de fungos. Quando uma jovem rainha sai para fundar uma nova colônia, ela leva na boca um pedacinho do fungo, como quem leva sementes para uma nova horta.
translation:
Anyone who walks along a trail in Brazil has probably seen a line of ants carrying pieces of leaves. They are saúvas, or leaf-cutter ants. Each one carries a piece of leaf much bigger than its own body. Many people think they eat these leaves, but that is not true.

The leaves go to the anthill, which can have hundreds of underground chambers. There, the ants chew the leaves and make a kind of paste. A fungus grows on this paste, and it is this fungus that feeds the colony. In other words, saúvas are farmers: they grow their own food, and they have been doing it for millions of years, long before human beings.

Each ant has a task. The biggest ones defend the nest, the medium-sized ones cut and carry the leaves, and the smallest ones look after the fungus garden. When a young queen leaves to start a new colony, she carries a little piece of the fungus in her mouth, like someone taking seeds to a new vegetable garden.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: How leaf-cutter ants really use the leaves they cut
Why leaf-cutter ants are dangerous for farmers
How people in Brazil protect their trees from ants
Why leaf-cutter ants prefer only green leaves
questions.explain: The passage follows the leaves from the trail into the nest and explains what the ants really do with them.

questions.q: What do the ants do with the leaves inside the nest?
options: They store them for the dry season
They chew them into a kind of paste
They use them to build the walls
They give them to the queen to eat
questions.explain: The text says 'as formigas mastigam as folhas e fazem uma espécie de massa'.

questions.q: According to the passage, what do the biggest ants do?
options: They cut the leaves
They carry the young queen
They look for water
They defend the nest
questions.explain: The text says 'As maiores defendem o ninho'.

questions.q: Why does a young queen carry a piece of fungus in her mouth?
options: To feed the ants of the old colony
To protect herself from bigger ants
To start a new fungus garden in her new nest
To show the other ants which leaves to cut
questions.explain: She carries it 'como quem leva sementes para uma nova horta', so she can grow food in the new colony.

topic: anonymous cakes for a retired teacher
title: Bolo às sextas
text:
Fazia dois meses que dona Lúcia, professora aposentada de Belo Horizonte, encontrava um bolo na porta de casa toda sexta-feira: de cenoura, de fubá, de laranja, sempre sem bilhete. Ela perguntou à vizinha, à sobrinha e ao carteiro, mas ninguém sabia de nada.

Numa sexta, ela acordou às cinco da manhã e ficou esperando atrás da janela. Pouco depois, apareceu um homem de uns quarenta anos, de avental branco, com um bolo nas mãos. Dona Lúcia abriu a porta antes que ele fosse embora. “A senhora não deve se lembrar de mim”, disse ele, envergonhado. “Sou o Rafael, da quarta série.”

Então ela se lembrou de um menino que tinha muita dificuldade para ler. Durante um ano, toda sexta-feira, ela ficava com ele depois da aula e, no fim, dividia com ele um pedaço de bolo. “Hoje tenho uma padaria”, contou Rafael. “Cada bolo é um obrigado.” Desde então, os bolos continuam chegando às sextas, mas agora Rafael entra para tomar um café.
translation:
For two months, Dona Lúcia, a retired teacher from Belo Horizonte, had been finding a cake at her front door every Friday: carrot, cornmeal, orange, always without a note. She asked her neighbour, her niece and the postman, but nobody knew anything.

One Friday, she woke up at five in the morning and waited behind the window. Soon after, a man of about forty appeared, in a white apron, with a cake in his hands. Dona Lúcia opened the door before he could leave. “You probably don't remember me,” he said, embarrassed. “I'm Rafael, from the fourth grade.”

Then she remembered a boy who had great difficulty reading. For a year, every Friday, she stayed with him after class and, at the end, shared a piece of cake with him. “Today I have a bakery,” Rafael said. “Each cake is a thank-you.” Since then, the cakes have kept arriving on Fridays, but now Rafael comes in for a coffee.

questions.q: What is the story mainly about?
options: A retired teacher who starts a cooking class
A neighbour who takes cakes from a door
A mystery about cakes and who leaves them
A girl who wins a cake contest at school
questions.explain: Dona Lúcia keeps finding cakes 'sempre sem bilhete' and finally discovers who brings them.

questions.q: What did Dona Lúcia do to find out who left the cakes?
options: She put a small camera above her door
She left a note asking for a name
She followed the postman for a whole day
She got up early and waited at the window
questions.explain: The text says 'ela acordou às cinco da manhã e ficou esperando atrás da janela'.

questions.q: What does Rafael do now?
options: He teaches at her old school
He runs his own bakery
He delivers letters in town
He writes books for children
questions.explain: Rafael says 'Hoje tenho uma padaria'.

questions.q: Why did Rafael leave the cakes?
options: To thank her for helping him as a child
To find out if she still lived there
To ask her to teach his son to read
To say sorry for being a lazy student
questions.explain: He says 'Cada bolo é um obrigado', and she remembers staying with him after class every Friday when he had trouble reading.

topic: public baths in ancient Rome
title: As termas de Roma
text:
Na Roma antiga, pouca gente tinha banheiro em casa. Por isso, quase todos os dias, ricos e pobres iam às termas, os banhos públicos da cidade. A entrada custava muito pouco, e algumas termas eram enormes: as de Caracalla, por exemplo, recebiam mais de mil pessoas ao mesmo tempo.

O banho seguia uma ordem. Primeiro, as pessoas faziam exercícios no pátio. Depois, passavam por salas cada vez mais quentes e, no fim, mergulhavam numa piscina fria. O calor vinha de grandes fornos: o ar quente circulava por baixo do chão, que ficava apoiado em pequenas colunas, e por dentro das paredes. Em vez de sabão, os romanos passavam azeite na pele e depois o tiravam com uma ferramenta de metal curva.

Mas as termas não serviam só para tomar banho. Eram lugares de encontro, como uma praça coberta. Lá, as pessoas conversavam, faziam negócios, liam na biblioteca, comiam petiscos vendidos por ambulantes e ouviam as últimas notícias da cidade.
translation:
In ancient Rome, few people had a bathroom at home. So, almost every day, rich and poor went to the thermae, the city's public baths. Entry cost very little, and some baths were enormous: those of Caracalla, for example, took in more than a thousand people at a time.

Bathing followed an order. First, people exercised in the courtyard. Then they went through hotter and hotter rooms and, at the end, plunged into a cold pool. The heat came from large furnaces: hot air circulated under the floor, which rested on small columns, and inside the walls. Instead of soap, the Romans spread olive oil on their skin and then removed it with a curved metal tool.

But the baths were not only for bathing. They were meeting places, like a covered square. There, people chatted, did business, read in the library, ate snacks sold by street vendors and heard the latest news of the city.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How the Romans built their private houses
The public baths and their role in Roman life
Why the Romans stopped going to the baths
The rich families who lived near Caracalla
questions.explain: The passage describes the 'termas', how a visit there worked and why they were meeting places.

questions.q: Why did most Romans go to the public baths?
options: Few of them had a bathroom at home
Doctors told them to bathe every day
It was the law for every citizen
The water there could cure illnesses
questions.explain: The text says 'pouca gente tinha banheiro em casa. Por isso... iam às termas'.

questions.q: How were the baths heated?
options: The sun warmed water tanks on the roofs
Workers carried hot stones into the rooms
Hot air from furnaces passed under the floor
Water came from hot springs under the city
questions.explain: The text says 'o ar quente circulava por baixo do chão... e por dentro das paredes'.

questions.q: In the last paragraph, what are “petiscos”?
options: Short books from the library
Warm towels for the bathers
Tickets to enter the baths
Small things to eat
questions.explain: People 'comiam petiscos vendidos por ambulantes', so petiscos are snacks that people ate.

topic: writer Machado de Assis
title: Machado de Assis
text:
Joaquim Maria Machado de Assis nasceu no Rio de Janeiro, em 1839, numa família pobre. Quase não frequentou a escola, mas adorava ler e aprendeu muito sozinho. Ainda adolescente, publicou os primeiros poemas e foi trabalhar numa tipografia, onde livros e jornais eram impressos. Ali, conheceu vários escritores.

Com o tempo, Machado escreveu de tudo: poesia, teatro, crônicas, contos e romances. Em 1881, publicou Memórias Póstumas de Brás Cubas, um livro muito original para a época, porque o narrador conta a própria vida depois de morto, com muita ironia e humor. Em 1897, ajudou a fundar a Academia Brasileira de Letras e foi o seu primeiro presidente.

Seu romance mais famoso, porém, é Dom Casmurro, de 1899. Nele, Bento Santiago narra a sua história com Capitu, o grande amor da sua vida, e desconfia que ela o enganou. O livro nunca dá a resposta. Por isso, mais de cem anos depois, os leitores ainda discutem: Capitu era culpada ou inocente?
translation:
Joaquim Maria Machado de Assis was born in Rio de Janeiro, in 1839, into a poor family. He hardly went to school, but he loved reading and learned a lot on his own. While still a teenager, he published his first poems and went to work in a print shop, where books and newspapers were printed. There, he met several writers.

Over time, Machado wrote everything: poetry, plays, newspaper columns, short stories and novels. In 1881, he published The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas, a very original book for its time, because the narrator tells the story of his own life after his death, with a lot of irony and humour. In 1897, he helped to found the Brazilian Academy of Letters and was its first president.

His most famous novel, however, is Dom Casmurro, from 1899. In it, Bento Santiago tells the story of his relationship with Capitu, the great love of his life, and suspects that she betrayed him. The book never gives the answer. That is why, more than a hundred years later, readers still argue: was Capitu guilty or innocent?

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The history of the Brazilian Academy of Letters
How books were printed in the 19th century
A love story that happened in Rio in 1899
The life and work of a great Brazilian writer
questions.explain: The passage follows Machado de Assis from his birth in 1839 to his most famous novel.

questions.q: What do we learn about Machado's education?
options: He studied literature at a university in Lisbon
He hardly went to school and learned on his own
His father taught him to read and write at home
He went to an expensive school paid by his family
questions.explain: The text says 'Quase não frequentou a escola, mas adorava ler e aprendeu muito sozinho'.

questions.q: What was unusual about Memórias Póstumas de Brás Cubas?
options: It was written by two different authors
It was the first book printed in Brazil
Its narrator tells his life after dying
It was written entirely in verse
questions.explain: The text says 'o narrador conta a própria vida depois de morto'.

questions.q: In the last paragraph, what does “desconfia” mean?
options: Thinks something is true but is not sure
Knows something for certain and can prove it
Forgets something that happened long ago
Decides to forgive someone he loves
questions.explain: Bento 'desconfia que ela o enganou', but 'O livro nunca dá a resposta': he suspects it without being sure.

topic: why the sky is blue
title: Por que o céu é azul?
text:
Por que o céu é azul? A resposta começa na luz do Sol. Ela parece branca, mas, na verdade, é uma mistura de todas as cores do arco-íris. Cada cor viaja como uma onda de tamanho diferente: a do vermelho é mais longa, e a do azul, mais curta.

Na atmosfera, a luz bate em pequenas partículas do ar, principalmente de nitrogênio e oxigênio. Essas partículas espalham a luz azul muito mais do que a vermelha. Assim, a luz azul se espalha por todo o céu e chega aos nossos olhos de todas as direções. Por isso, quando olhamos para cima, vemos azul.

No fim da tarde, a situação muda. Com o Sol perto do horizonte, a luz atravessa uma camada de ar muito mais grossa, e quase todo o azul se perde no caminho. Sobram o laranja e o vermelho, as cores do pôr do sol. E na Lua, onde não há atmosfera, o céu é preto mesmo durante o dia.
translation:
Why is the sky blue? The answer begins with sunlight. It looks white but is actually a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow. Each colour travels as a wave of a different size: red's is longer, and blue's is shorter.

In the atmosphere, light hits tiny particles of air, mainly of nitrogen and oxygen. These particles scatter blue light much more than red. So blue light spreads across the whole sky and reaches our eyes from every direction. That is why, when we look up, we see blue.

At the end of the afternoon, the situation changes. With the Sun near the horizon, the light crosses a much thicker layer of air, and almost all the blue is lost on the way. Orange and red remain, the colours of the sunset. And on the Moon, where there is no atmosphere, the sky is black even during the day.

questions.q: What does the passage mainly explain?
options: Why the sky has the colours we see
How a rainbow appears after the rain
Why the Moon has no atmosphere
How the Sun produces its light
questions.explain: The passage asks 'Por que o céu é azul?' and also explains why the sky changes colour at sunset.

questions.q: According to the passage, what is sunlight made of?
options: Only blue and red light waves
Small particles of oxygen and nitrogen
A mix of all the colours of the rainbow
White light without any other colours
questions.explain: The text says sunlight 'é uma mistura de todas as cores do arco-íris'.

questions.q: What do the particles of air do with blue light?
options: They absorb it so that it disappears
They turn it into orange and red light
They let it pass straight through
They spread it much more than red light
questions.explain: The text says 'Essas partículas espalham a luz azul muito mais do que a vermelha'.

questions.q: Why does the passage mention the Moon at the end?
options: To show that the Moon reflects sunlight
To show that air is what makes the sky blue
To explain why sunsets are orange and red
To explain how the Moon changes its shape
questions.explain: Where there is no atmosphere, the sky is black, so the blue must come from the air.

topic: fable of the fireflies and the Moon
title: A Lua e os vaga-lumes
text:
Numa floresta do interior, a Lua gostava de se exibir. Toda noite, ela iluminava as árvores, o rio e as pedras, e ria dos vaga-lumes. “Para que essas luzinhas?”, perguntava. “Eu ilumino a floresta inteira, e vocês não iluminam nem uma folha.” Os vaga-lumes ficavam tristes, mas continuavam piscando, cada um no seu canto.

Uma noite, nuvens escuras cobriram o céu, e a Lua desapareceu. Justamente nessa noite, um filhote de tatu se perdeu longe da toca. Ele chorava baixinho, sem enxergar nada, quando um vaga-lume pousou perto dele. Logo chegaram outros. Juntos, centenas de vaga-lumes formaram um caminho de luz entre as árvores, e o tatuzinho voltou para casa em segurança.

Na noite seguinte, a Lua apareceu de novo, mas não riu de ninguém. Tinha visto tudo por trás das nuvens. Desde então, quando os vaga-lumes piscam, ela brilha um pouco menos, para que as luzinhas também possam ser vistas. Afinal, nenhuma luz é pequena demais para quem está no escuro.
translation:
In a forest in the countryside, the Moon liked to show off. Every night, she lit up the trees, the river and the rocks, and laughed at the fireflies. “What are these little lights for?” she would ask. “I light up the whole forest, and you don't even light up a single leaf.” The fireflies were sad, but they kept on blinking, each one in its own corner.

One night, dark clouds covered the sky, and the Moon disappeared. That very night, a baby armadillo got lost far from its burrow. It was crying quietly, unable to see anything, when a firefly landed near it. Soon others arrived. Together, hundreds of fireflies formed a path of light between the trees, and the little armadillo got home safely.

The next night, the Moon appeared again, but she didn't laugh at anyone. She had seen everything from behind the clouds. Since then, when the fireflies blink, she shines a little less, so that the little lights can be seen too. After all, no light is too small for someone who is in the dark.

questions.q: What is the main lesson of the fable?
options: The strongest light always wins in the end
Animals should not walk alone at night
Even a small light can be very important
Fireflies should stay away from the Moon
questions.explain: The fable ends: 'nenhuma luz é pequena demais para quem está no escuro'.

questions.q: Why was the forest so dark that night?
options: The fireflies had gone to sleep
The Moon was angry and hid
Dark clouds covered the sky
The armadillo went into a cave
questions.explain: The text says 'nuvens escuras cobriram o céu, e a Lua desapareceu'.

questions.q: How did the fireflies help the baby armadillo?
options: They made a path of light through the trees
They flew off to call the Moon back
They carried it on their backs to the burrow
They stayed next to it until the morning
questions.explain: The text says 'centenas de vaga-lumes formaram um caminho de luz entre as árvores'.

questions.q: In the first sentence, what does “se exibir” mean?
options: To stay quiet and hidden
To show off to others
To sleep during the day
To travel across the sky
questions.explain: The Moon lit up everything and laughed at the fireflies' small lights: she liked to show everyone how bright she was.

topic: Inca roads and chasqui runners
title: As estradas dos incas
text:
No século XV, os incas governavam um enorme império na Cordilheira dos Andes, na América do Sul. Para ligar as suas cidades, eles construíram uma rede de estradas com mais de 30 mil quilômetros, que atravessava montanhas, desertos e florestas. Os incas não usavam cavalos nem carroças com rodas: as pessoas andavam a pé, e as lhamas carregavam as mercadorias.

As notícias viajavam com os chasquis, jovens corredores muito bem treinados. Cada chasqui corria alguns quilômetros até um pequeno posto na estrada, onde outro corredor esperava. Ele repetia a mensagem, que tinha decorado, e o segundo saía correndo. Dessa forma, uma notícia podia percorrer mais de 200 quilômetros em um único dia. Para os números, eles usavam os quipus, cordões coloridos com nós.

Nos vales mais profundos, os incas construíram pontes suspensas feitas de capim trançado. Uma delas, a ponte Q'eswachaka, no Peru, é refeita todos os anos pelos moradores da região, com a mesma técnica de séculos atrás.
translation:
In the 15th century, the Incas ruled a huge empire in the Andes mountains, in South America. To connect their cities, they built a network of roads more than 30,000 kilometres long, which crossed mountains, deserts and forests. The Incas did not use horses or carts with wheels: people walked, and llamas carried the goods.

News was carried by the chasquis, very well-trained young runners. Each chasqui ran a few kilometres to a small post on the road, where another runner was waiting. He repeated the message, which he had learned by heart, and the second one set off running. In this way, a piece of news could travel more than 200 kilometres in a single day. For numbers, they used quipus, coloured cords with knots.

In the deepest valleys, the Incas built suspension bridges made of woven grass. One of them, the Q'eswachaka bridge, in Peru, is rebuilt every year by the people of the region, with the same technique as centuries ago.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The wild animals that live high in the Andes
How the Incas connected their huge empire
Why the Incas built their cities so high
The modern highways of Peru and Chile
questions.explain: The passage describes how the Incas built roads and bridges and sent news across their empire.

questions.q: How did a message travel along the roads?
options: Riders carried it on fast horses
It was sent with smoke from hill to hill
One runner carried it all the way alone
Runners passed it on from one to another
questions.explain: Each chasqui ran to a post 'onde outro corredor esperava', repeated the message, and the next one ran on.

questions.q: What were quipus used for?
options: Building bridges over valleys
Carrying goods on long trips
Making clothes for the runners
Recording numbers with knots
questions.explain: The text says 'Para os números, eles usavam os quipus, cordões coloridos com nós'.

questions.q: What can we conclude about the Q'eswachaka bridge?
options: The Inca way of building it has not been forgotten
It is made of stone and will last for centuries
It was designed by modern engineers last year
It is the longest bridge in South America
questions.explain: It 'é refeita todos os anos... com a mesma técnica de séculos atrás', so people still know the old technique.

topic: the cavaquinho and the ukulele
title: Do cavaquinho ao ukulele
titleEn: From the Cavaquinho to the Ukulele
text:
O cavaquinho é um instrumento pequeno, de quatro cordas, que nasceu no norte de Portugal. Levado para o Brasil pelos portugueses, ele se tornou essencial na música brasileira: é difícil imaginar uma roda de samba ou de choro sem o seu som alegre.

Mas a história do cavaquinho não termina aí. Em 1879, um navio chegou ao Havaí trazendo centenas de imigrantes da Ilha da Madeira, que iam trabalhar nas plantações de cana-de-açúcar. Na bagagem, alguns deles levavam um instrumento muito parecido com o cavaquinho. Conta-se que um dos imigrantes começou a tocar canções da sua terra ainda no porto, e os havaianos ficaram encantados.

Em pouco tempo, o instrumento conquistou o Havaí e ganhou um novo nome: ukulele. Segundo uma explicação famosa, a palavra significa “pulga que pula” em havaiano, por causa dos dedos rápidos dos músicos sobre as cordas. Hoje, o ukulele é tocado no mundo inteiro, e muita gente nem imagina que ele é primo do nosso cavaquinho.
translation:
The cavaquinho is a small four-string instrument that originated in the north of Portugal. Taken to Brazil by the Portuguese, it became essential in Brazilian music: it is hard to imagine a samba or choro circle without its cheerful sound.

But the story of the cavaquinho doesn't end there. In 1879, a ship arrived in Hawaii carrying hundreds of immigrants from the island of Madeira, who were going to work on the sugar cane plantations. In their luggage, some of them carried an instrument very similar to the cavaquinho. It is said that one of the immigrants started playing songs from his homeland while still at the port, and the Hawaiians were delighted.

In a short time, the instrument won over Hawaii and got a new name: ukulele. According to a famous explanation, the word means “jumping flea” in Hawaiian, because of the musicians' quick fingers on the strings. Today, the ukulele is played all over the world, and many people have no idea that it is a cousin of our cavaquinho.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The travels of a small Portuguese instrument
How to play samba on the cavaquinho
How the Hawaiian language was created
Why Hawaiian music is popular in Brazil
questions.explain: The passage follows the cavaquinho from the north of Portugal to Brazil and much farther away.

questions.q: Why did the immigrants from Madeira go to Hawaii?
options: To open shops that sold instruments
To work on sugar cane plantations
To study music at a famous school
To visit family who lived there
questions.explain: The immigrants 'iam trabalhar nas plantações de cana-de-açúcar'.

questions.q: According to a famous story, what happened when the ship arrived?
options: The Hawaiians gave the immigrants a party
The immigrants sold all their instruments
An immigrant played songs from home at the port
A Hawaiian taught the newcomers a local song
questions.explain: 'Conta-se que um dos imigrantes começou a tocar canções da sua terra ainda no porto'.

questions.q: What does “o instrumento conquistou o Havaí” mean?
options: It was sent back to Madeira
It won a famous music contest
It became very popular there
It was sold only to rich people
questions.explain: 'Em pouco tempo', the instrument was loved all over Hawaii and even got a Hawaiian name.

topic: how taste and smell work together
title: O mapa errado da língua
titleEn: The Wrong Map of the Tongue
text:
Durante muitos anos, os livros escolares mostravam um “mapa da língua”: o doce ficava na ponta, o amargo no fundo, e o salgado e o azedo nos lados. Hoje sabemos que esse mapa está errado. As papilas gustativas, que percebem os sabores, estão espalhadas pela língua, e cada região consegue sentir todos os gostos.

Os cientistas reconhecem cinco gostos básicos: doce, salgado, azedo, amargo e umami. O último foi descoberto em 1908 pelo químico japonês Kikunae Ikeda, que queria entender o sabor especial de um caldo de algas. Em japonês, umami quer dizer algo como “gosto delicioso”, e ele aparece em alimentos como tomate maduro, queijo e cogumelos.

Mas a língua não trabalha sozinha. Grande parte do que chamamos de sabor vem do nariz. Por isso, quando estamos resfriados, a comida parece não ter gosto. Faça um teste: tape o nariz e coma um pedaço de maçã. Sem o cheiro, é difícil saber que fruta você está comendo.
translation:
For many years, school books showed a “tongue map”: sweet was at the tip, bitter at the back, and salty and sour on the sides. Today we know that this map is wrong. The taste buds, which perceive flavours, are spread across the tongue, and each area can sense all the tastes.

Scientists recognise five basic tastes: sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami. The last one was discovered in 1908 by the Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda, who wanted to understand the special flavour of a seaweed broth. In Japanese, umami means something like “delicious taste”, and it is found in foods such as ripe tomatoes, cheese and mushrooms.

But the tongue doesn't work alone. A large part of what we call flavour comes from the nose. That is why, when we have a cold, food seems to have no taste. Try a test: hold your nose and eat a piece of apple. Without the smell, it is hard to tell which fruit you are eating.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why some people do not like bitter food
How chefs make food look beautiful
Why apples are sweeter than other fruits
How we really sense the taste of food
questions.explain: The whole passage is about how we perceive tastes and flavours.

questions.q: What is wrong with the old “tongue map”?
options: Every area of the tongue can sense all tastes
Taste buds are found only at the tip of the tongue
The tongue cannot sense bitter food at all
Salty food is sensed only in the middle
questions.explain: Taste buds 'estão espalhadas pela língua, e cada região consegue sentir todos os gostos'.

questions.q: What did Kikunae Ikeda want to understand?
options: Why tomatoes turn red when they ripen
The special flavour of a seaweed soup
Why sugar dissolves faster in hot water
How cheese gets its strong flavour
questions.explain: Ikeda 'queria entender o sabor especial de um caldo de algas'.

questions.q: What can we conclude from the apple test?
options: Apples have no taste at all
The tongue cannot sense sweet things
Apples should be eaten without smelling them
Smell helps us recognise what we are eating
questions.explain: Without the smell, 'é difícil saber que fruta você está comendo', so the nose helps us identify flavours.

topic: a rhyming fruit seller loses his voice
title: O vendedor de rimas
text:
Na feira de domingo do bairro, todo mundo conhecia seu Raimundo, o vendedor de frutas que falava rimando. “Olha a manga, freguesa, é doce que é uma beleza!”, gritava ele. “Laranja pra suco, só não leva quem é maluco!” As pessoas riam, paravam na barraca e sempre levavam alguma coisa.

Mas, num domingo de chuva, seu Raimundo acordou sem voz. Mesmo assim, foi para a feira, arrumou as frutas e ficou sentado, em silêncio, atrás da barraca. “Hoje não vendo nada”, pensou, triste. Os fregueses passavam e estranhavam aquele silêncio.

De repente, dona Teresa, uma freguesa de muitos anos, subiu num caixote e gritou: “Olha a manga, freguesa, é doce que é uma beleza!” Uma criança continuou: “Laranja pra suco...” E metade da feira respondeu, rindo: “Só não leva quem é maluco!” Logo havia fila na barraca, e ao meio-dia não sobrava nem uma banana. Emocionado, seu Raimundo sussurrou a rima mais bonita do dia: “Obrigado, freguesia, vocês são a minha alegria.”
translation:
At the neighbourhood's Sunday market, everybody knew Seu Raimundo, the fruit seller who spoke in rhymes. “Look at the mangoes, madam, they're sweet and a real beauty!” he would shout. “Oranges for juice, only a fool says no!” People laughed, stopped at the stall and always bought something.

But one rainy Sunday, Seu Raimundo woke up without his voice. Even so, he went to the market, arranged the fruit and sat in silence behind the stall. “I won't sell anything today,” he thought sadly. The customers walked past and found that silence strange.

Suddenly, Dona Teresa, a customer of many years, climbed onto a crate and shouted: “Look at the mangoes, madam, they're sweet and a real beauty!” A child went on: “Oranges for juice...” And half the market answered, laughing: “Only a fool says no!” Soon there was a queue at the stall, and by noon there wasn't a single banana left. Moved, Seu Raimundo whispered the most beautiful rhyme of the day: “Thank you, dear customers, you are my joy.”

questions.q: What is the story mainly about?
options: A child who wants to sell fruit at a market
A seller who loses his stall in the rain
A market that helps its favourite seller
A woman who opens a new fruit stall
questions.explain: The story shows how the people at the market help Seu Raimundo on a difficult day.

questions.q: Why was Seu Raimundo sitting in silence?
options: He was angry with his customers
He woke up without his voice
The market had no customers that day
He had forgotten all his rhymes
questions.explain: The text says 'seu Raimundo acordou sem voz'.

questions.q: What did Dona Teresa do?
options: She stood on a crate and shouted his rhyme
She sold her own fruit next to his stall
She helped him carry the fruit home
She asked the children to be quiet
questions.explain: The text says she 'subiu num caixote e gritou: “Olha a manga, freguesa...”'.

questions.q: What does “não sobrava nem uma banana” tell us?
options: He forgot to bring bananas that day
Bananas were the only fruit he sold
The customers did not like bananas
He had sold everything by noon
questions.explain: There was a queue, and 'ao meio-dia não sobrava nem uma banana': all the fruit was sold.

topic: the golden age of Brazilian radio
title: A era de ouro do rádio
text:
O rádio chegou oficialmente ao Brasil em 7 de setembro de 1922, durante a festa dos cem anos da Independência, no Rio de Janeiro. Nessa ocasião, foram transmitidos um discurso e uma ópera, mas o rádio ainda era novidade: quase ninguém tinha um aparelho.

Com o tempo, isso mudou. Nas décadas de 1940 e 1950, a chamada “era de ouro do rádio”, o aparelho ocupava o lugar de honra da sala. À noite, as famílias se reuniam em volta dele para ouvir música, programas de humor, futebol e, principalmente, radionovelas. A primeira, Em Busca da Felicidade, estreou em 1941 e fez enorme sucesso.

Sem imagens, tudo dependia do som. Nos estúdios, uma equipe criava os efeitos ao vivo: cascas de coco batendo numa mesa imitavam os passos de um cavalo, e papel celofane amassado parecia o barulho do fogo. Quem ouvia usava a imaginação para completar a cena. Nos anos 1950, porém, a televisão chegou e, aos poucos, roubou a atenção do público.
translation:
Radio officially arrived in Brazil on 7 September 1922, during the celebrations of the centenary of Independence, in Rio de Janeiro. On that occasion, a speech and an opera were broadcast, but radio was still a novelty: almost nobody had a radio set.

Over time, that changed. In the 1940s and 1950s, the so-called “golden age of radio”, the set had the place of honour in the living room. In the evening, families gathered around it to listen to music, comedy shows, football and, above all, radio soap operas. The first one, In Search of Happiness, premiered in 1941 and was a huge success.

Without pictures, everything depended on sound. In the studios, a team created the effects live: coconut shells knocking on a table imitated a horse's hooves, and crumpled cellophane sounded like fire. Listeners used their imagination to complete the scene. In the 1950s, however, television arrived and, little by little, stole the public's attention.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How to build a radio set at home
The years when radio was most popular in Brazil
The life of a famous Brazilian radio singer
How radio signals travel through the air
questions.explain: The passage describes the 'era de ouro do rádio', when the radio had 'o lugar de honra da sala'.

questions.q: What was true of radio in Brazil in 1922?
options: It was already in most living rooms
It could be heard only in São Paulo
Almost nobody had a radio set yet
Its programmes were mostly about football
questions.explain: The text says that in 1922 'o rádio ainda era novidade: quase ninguém tinha um aparelho'.

questions.q: How did studio teams make the sound of a horse?
options: By recording real horses on farms
By hitting a drum very softly
By clapping their hands slowly
By knocking coconut shells on a table
questions.explain: The text says 'cascas de coco batendo numa mesa imitavam os passos de um cavalo'.

questions.q: What does “roubou a atenção do público” mean here?
options: People slowly began to prefer television
Television copied all the radio programmes
Radio programmes became more popular than ever
People stopped paying for their radio sets
questions.explain: When television arrived, 'aos poucos' it took listeners' interest away from radio.

topic: false friends between Portuguese and Spanish
title: Cuidado com os falsos amigos
text:
Português e espanhol são línguas muito parecidas. Um brasileiro que viaja pela América do Sul entende grande parte do que ouve e, muitas vezes, consegue se comunicar misturando as duas línguas, no famoso “portunhol”. Mas é preciso ter cuidado com os falsos amigos: palavras que parecem iguais, mas têm significados diferentes.

Imagine um turista brasileiro num restaurante em Lima, no Peru. O garçom recomenda uma torta e diz que ela é “exquisita”. O turista fica preocupado, porque, em português, “esquisito” quer dizer estranho. Mas, em espanhol, a palavra significa deliciosa. Depois, um amigo peruano pede: “Espera un rato”. O brasileiro olha para o chão, procurando um rato, mas o amigo só queria que ele esperasse um pouco.

Há muitos outros exemplos. “Polvo”, para nós, é um animal do mar, mas, em espanhol, é poeira. E “embarazada” não é “embaraçada”: quer dizer grávida! Por isso, os professores sempre repetem: parecido não quer dizer igual.
translation:
Portuguese and Spanish are very similar languages. A Brazilian travelling around South America understands a large part of what he hears and, very often, can communicate by mixing the two languages, in the famous “portunhol”. But you have to be careful with false friends: words that look the same but have different meanings.

Imagine a Brazilian tourist in a restaurant in Lima, Peru. The waiter recommends a cake and says it is “exquisita”. The tourist gets worried, because in Portuguese “esquisito” means strange. But in Spanish the word means delicious. Later, a Peruvian friend asks: “Espera un rato”. The Brazilian looks at the floor, searching for a rat, but his friend only wanted him to wait a little.

There are many other examples. “Polvo”, for us, is a sea animal (an octopus), but in Spanish it is dust. And “embarazada” is not “embaraçada” (embarrassed): it means pregnant! That is why teachers always repeat: similar does not mean the same.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Some similar words have different meanings
Brazilians cannot understand Spanish at all
Spanish is easier to learn than Portuguese
Restaurants in Lima serve the best desserts
questions.explain: The passage warns about 'falsos amigos: palavras que parecem iguais, mas têm significados diferentes'.

questions.q: Why did the tourist get worried in the restaurant?
options: The cake was too expensive for him
The waiter did not speak Portuguese
He did not like the taste of the cake
He understood that the cake was strange
questions.explain: The text says that in Portuguese 'esquisito' quer dizer estranho, so he thought the cake was strange.

questions.q: What did the Peruvian friend want when he said “Espera un rato”?
options: He wanted to show him a rat
He wanted him to wait a little
He wanted him to look at the floor
He wanted to order another cake
questions.explain: The text says 'o amigo só queria que ele esperasse um pouco'.

questions.q: In the first paragraph, what is “portunhol”?
options: A language spoken only in Peru
A dictionary of false friends
A mix of Portuguese and Spanish
A popular South American dessert
questions.explain: Brazilians communicate 'misturando as duas línguas, no famoso portunhol'.

topic: the meeting of the waters near Manaus
title: O Encontro das Águas
text:
Perto de Manaus, acontece um espetáculo que atrai turistas do mundo inteiro: o Encontro das Águas. Ali, o Rio Negro, de água escura, encontra o Rio Solimões, de cor barrenta, parecida com café com leite. O curioso é que as duas águas não se misturam logo. Durante vários quilômetros, elas correm lado a lado, como se uma linha separasse os dois rios.

A explicação está nas diferenças entre eles. O Rio Negro é mais quente e corre mais devagar. A cor escura vem de folhas que se decompõem na água, como num chá. Já o Solimões é mais frio, mais rápido e traz muita areia e lama da Cordilheira dos Andes, o que torna a sua água mais pesada.

Mais adiante, as correntes acabam misturando tudo, e o rio que nasce desse encontro passa a se chamar Amazonas. Quem faz o passeio de barco pode até colocar uma mão em cada lado da linha e sentir a diferença de temperatura.
translation:
Near Manaus, there is a spectacle that attracts tourists from all over the world: the Meeting of the Waters. There, the Rio Negro, with its dark water, meets the Rio Solimões, which has a muddy colour, similar to milky coffee. The curious thing is that the two waters don't mix right away. For several kilometres, they flow side by side, as if a line separated the two rivers.

The explanation lies in the differences between them. The Rio Negro is warmer and flows more slowly. Its dark colour comes from leaves that decompose in the water, as in a tea. The Solimões, on the other hand, is colder, faster and carries a lot of sand and mud from the Andes, which makes its water heavier.

Further on, the currents end up mixing everything, and the river born from this meeting is then called the Amazon. Anyone who takes the boat trip can even put one hand on each side of the line and feel the difference in temperature.

questions.q: What does the passage mainly describe?
options: How the city of Manaus was built
Why tourists like boat trips on rivers
How the Amazon River reaches the sea
Two rivers that meet but don't mix at first
questions.explain: The passage is about the 'Encontro das Águas' of the Rio Negro and the Rio Solimões and explains why it happens.

questions.q: Where does the dark colour of the Rio Negro come from?
options: From leaves that rot in the water
From black sand at the bottom
From the dark clay of its banks
From the shadow of the tall trees
questions.explain: The text says 'A cor escura vem de folhas que se decompõem na água'.

questions.q: Which is true of the Solimões, according to the passage?
options: It is warmer and slower than the Rio Negro
It carries very little sand or mud
It is colder and faster than the Rio Negro
It begins in the forest near Manaus
questions.explain: The text says 'o Solimões é mais frio, mais rápido e traz muita areia e lama'.

questions.q: What does “como se uma linha separasse os dois rios” suggest?
options: There is a wall built between the rivers
You can see clearly where each water ends
The rivers are kept apart by a sandbank
Boats cannot cross from one river to the other
questions.explain: The waters 'correm lado a lado' without mixing, so the border between the two colours is easy to see.

topic: a bored teenager discovers the night sky
title: O céu do sítio
text:
Quando os pais avisaram que ele ia passar as férias no sítio dos avós, em Goiás, Lucas, de quatorze anos, ficou furioso. No sítio não havia internet, e o celular não pegava. Nos dois primeiros dias, ele quase não saiu do quarto e respondia a tudo com “tanto faz”.

Na terceira noite, o avô apagou todas as luzes da casa e chamou: “Vem cá fora, quero te mostrar uma coisa.” Lucas foi, de má vontade. Mas, quando levantou os olhos, ficou sem palavras. O céu estava coberto de estrelas, e uma faixa clara o atravessava de um lado ao outro. “É a Via Láctea”, explicou o avô. “Na cidade, as luzes não deixam a gente ver.”

Daquela noite em diante, avô e neto se deitavam na grama para observar o céu. O avô ensinou Lucas a achar o sul usando quatro estrelas em forma de pipa. Quando as férias terminaram, foi o próprio Lucas quem pediu para voltar no ano seguinte.
translation:
When his parents told him he was going to spend the holidays at his grandparents' small farm, in Goiás, fourteen-year-old Lucas was furious. At the farm there was no internet, and his phone had no signal. For the first two days, he hardly left his room and answered everything with “whatever”.

On the third night, his grandfather turned off all the lights in the house and called: “Come outside, I want to show you something.” Lucas went, reluctantly. But when he looked up, he was speechless. The sky was covered with stars, and a pale band crossed it from one side to the other. “It's the Milky Way,” his grandfather explained. “In the city, the lights don't let us see it.”

From that night on, grandfather and grandson would lie on the grass to watch the sky. His grandfather taught Lucas to find the south using four stars in the shape of a kite. When the holidays ended, it was Lucas himself who asked to come back the next year.

questions.q: What is the story mainly about?
options: A boy who gets lost on his grandparents' farm
A grandfather who moves to the big city
A teenager who discovers the night sky
A family that buys a farm without internet
questions.explain: The story builds up to the night when Lucas's grandfather takes him outside to look at the sky.

questions.q: Why was Lucas furious at the beginning?
options: His grandparents did not want him there
His parents took his phone away
He had to study during the holidays
He had to spend his holidays on a farm
questions.explain: He got furious when his parents said 'ele ia passar as férias no sítio dos avós'.

questions.q: What crossed the sky from one side to the other?
options: The Milky Way
A long line of clouds
The light of a plane
Smoke from the kitchen
questions.explain: The grandfather explains: 'É a Via Láctea'.

questions.q: What does Lucas mean when he answers everything with “tanto faz”?
options: He is very happy to be there
He does not care about anything
He wants to help on the farm
He is too tired to speak
questions.explain: Lucas was furious and hardly left his room, so “tanto faz” shows that nothing interested him.

topic: Hercule Florence, photography pioneer in Brazil
title: O inventor esquecido
text:
Em 1824, um jovem francês chamado Hercule Florence chegou ao Rio de Janeiro. Pouco depois, participou como desenhista de uma longa expedição pelo interior do Brasil e, no fim da viagem, decidiu ficar no país. Casou-se e foi morar em Campinas, no interior de São Paulo.

Na pequena cidade, não havia nenhuma tipografia. Florence precisava reproduzir textos e desenhos e começou a fazer experiências. Por volta de 1833, usando uma câmara escura e papel coberto com nitrato de prata, uma substância que escurece com a luz, ele conseguiu fixar imagens no papel. Nos seus cadernos, chamou a descoberta de “photographie”, palavra que só ficaria conhecida na Europa anos depois.

Em 1839, o francês Louis Daguerre apresentou em Paris o seu invento, e o mundo celebrou o nascimento da fotografia. Florence, isolado no interior do Brasil, continuou desconhecido. Só nos anos 1970 um pesquisador estudou os seus cadernos e mostrou que ele tinha sido um dos verdadeiros pioneiros da fotografia.
translation:
In 1824, a young Frenchman called Hercule Florence arrived in Rio de Janeiro. Soon after, he took part as an illustrator in a long expedition through the interior of Brazil and, at the end of the journey, decided to stay in the country. He got married and went to live in Campinas, in the interior of São Paulo.

In the small town, there was no print shop at all. Florence needed to reproduce texts and drawings and began to experiment. Around 1833, using a camera obscura and paper coated with silver nitrate, a substance that darkens with light, he managed to fix images on paper. In his notebooks, he called the discovery “photographie”, a word that would only become known in Europe years later.

In 1839, the Frenchman Louis Daguerre presented his invention in Paris, and the world celebrated the birth of photography. Florence, isolated in the interior of Brazil, remained unknown. Only in the 1970s did a researcher study his notebooks and show that he had been one of the true pioneers of photography.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The life and work of Louis Daguerre in Paris
A forgotten pioneer of photography in Brazil
How to take photos with a very old camera
The early history of the city of Campinas
questions.explain: The passage tells the story of Hercule Florence, whose early work in photography stayed unknown for many years.

questions.q: Why did Florence start doing experiments?
options: His town had no print shop
He wanted to sell cameras
A French scientist asked him to
He wanted to become famous in Paris
questions.explain: The text says 'não havia nenhuma tipografia' and that he 'precisava reproduzir textos e desenhos'.

questions.q: What did Florence use to fix images on paper?
options: Ink and wooden blocks he carved
Paint and brushes made in Brazil
Glass plates and a strong lamp
A camera obscura and silver nitrate
questions.explain: He used 'uma câmara escura e papel coberto com nitrato de prata'.

questions.q: What does the passage suggest about the invention of photography?
options: Daguerre copied Florence's own notebooks
It was invented in Paris and nowhere else
It was discovered in more than one place
Florence learned the method from Daguerre
questions.explain: Florence fixed images around 1833 in Brazil, and Daguerre presented his own invention in Paris in 1839.

topic: chimarrão drinking customs in southern Brazil
title: A roda de chimarrão
text:
No Rio Grande do Sul, muita gente anda pela rua com uma garrafa térmica e uma cuia na mão. Dentro da cuia está o chimarrão, uma bebida quente e amarga feita com folhas de erva-mate. Os guaranis já tomavam essa bebida antes da chegada dos europeus, e o costume continua forte no Sul do Brasil e nos países vizinhos.

Tomar chimarrão é um ritual social, com regras próprias. A pessoa que prepara a bebida toma a primeira cuia, que é a mais amarga. Depois, coloca mais água quente e passa a cuia para o próximo da roda. Cada um bebe toda a água pela bomba, um canudo de metal, e devolve a cuia a quem serve.

Os visitantes devem saber duas coisas. Primeiro, não se deve mexer na bomba, porque ela pode entupir. Segundo, dizer “obrigado” não é só educação: significa que você não quer mais. Muitos turistas agradecem logo na primeira vez e não entendem por que a cuia nunca mais volta.
translation:
In Rio Grande do Sul, many people walk down the street with a thermos flask and a gourd in their hand. Inside the gourd is chimarrão, a hot, bitter drink made with yerba mate leaves. The Guarani already drank it before the Europeans arrived, and the custom is still strong in southern Brazil and in the neighbouring countries.

Drinking chimarrão is a social ritual, with its own rules. The person who prepares the drink has the first gourdful, which is the most bitter. Then they add more hot water and pass the gourd to the next person in the circle. Each person drinks all the water through the bomba, a metal straw, and gives the gourd back to the one who is serving.

Visitors should know two things. First, you shouldn't move the bomba, because it can get blocked. Second, saying “thank you” is not just good manners: it means you don't want any more. Many tourists say thank you the very first time and don't understand why the gourd never comes back.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: A traditional drink and the customs around it
How yerba mate is grown and harvested
The history of the Guarani people
Why tourists like to visit southern Brazil
questions.explain: The passage describes chimarrão, where people drink it and the rules for sharing it.

questions.q: Who drinks the first gourd of chimarrão?
options: The oldest person in the circle
The visitor or guest of honour
The person who prepares it
The youngest person present
questions.explain: The text says 'A pessoa que prepara a bebida toma a primeira cuia'.

questions.q: Why shouldn't you move the bomba?
options: Because it is hot and can burn you
Because it can get blocked
Because it belongs to the host
Because it can break the gourd
questions.explain: The text says 'não se deve mexer na bomba, porque ela pode entupir'.

questions.q: Why does the gourd never come back to many tourists?
options: They drank too slowly for the others
They did not sit in the circle
They did not drink all the water
Their thank-you meant they had finished
questions.explain: Saying 'obrigado' 'significa que você não quer mais', so tourists who say it at once are not served again.

topic: Magellanic penguins on Brazilian beaches
title: Pinguins no Brasil
text:
Todos os anos, no inverno, os moradores do litoral de Santa Catarina e do Rio Grande do Sul recebem visitantes inesperados: pinguins. São pinguins-de-magalhães, que vivem na Patagônia, no sul da Argentina e do Chile. Nessa época, eles nadam milhares de quilômetros para o norte, seguindo os cardumes de peixes que comem.

Durante a longa viagem, alguns pinguins, quase sempre jovens que fazem a migração pela primeira vez, ficam cansados e fracos. As correntes do oceano os levam até as praias brasileiras, onde eles param para descansar. Às vezes, aparecem até no Rio de Janeiro.

Quem encontra um pinguim na areia quer ajudar, mas muitas vezes erra. Como acham que o animal está sofrendo com o calor, algumas pessoas o colocam no congelador ou lhe dão gelo, o que é muito perigoso para ele. Os especialistas recomendam não tocar no animal, não dar comida e chamar os serviços de resgate. Depois de tratados, os pinguins são devolvidos ao mar e voltam para casa.
translation:
Every year, in winter, people living on the coast of Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul receive unexpected visitors: penguins. They are Magellanic penguins, which live in Patagonia, in the south of Argentina and Chile. At this time of year, they swim thousands of kilometres north, following the shoals of fish they eat.

During the long journey, some penguins, almost always young ones migrating for the first time, become tired and weak. Ocean currents carry them to Brazilian beaches, where they stop to rest. Sometimes they even appear in Rio de Janeiro.

People who find a penguin on the sand want to help, but they often get it wrong. Because they think the animal is suffering from the heat, some people put it in the freezer or give it ice, which is very dangerous for it. Experts recommend not touching the animal, not feeding it and calling the rescue services. After treatment, the penguins are returned to the sea and go back home.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why penguins cannot live in Patagonia
How to keep a penguin as a pet at home
The fish that live along the Brazilian coast
Penguins that reach Brazil and how to help them
questions.explain: The passage tells how penguins come to Brazil in winter and how people should act when they find one.

questions.q: Why do the penguins swim north in winter?
options: To find warmer beaches to rest on
To follow the fish they eat
To build their nests in Brazil
To escape from bigger animals
questions.explain: They swim north 'seguindo os cardumes de peixes que comem'.

questions.q: Which penguins usually end up on Brazilian beaches?
options: Young ones migrating for the first time
Old penguins that cannot swim any more
Mothers looking for food for their chicks
Penguins that were born in Brazil
questions.explain: The text says they are 'quase sempre jovens que fazem a migração pela primeira vez'.

questions.q: What can we conclude about people who put penguins in the freezer?
options: They want to keep the penguin as a pet
They are following the experts' advice
They want to help but do the wrong thing
They think the penguin is too cold
questions.explain: They do it because 'acham que o animal está sofrendo com o calor', but it 'é muito perigoso para ele'.
